title: How to Evaluate Managed WiFi Contracts in 2026
summary: Learn how to evaluate managed WiFi contracts for multifamily properties. Covers SLAs, support models, ownership terms, and what property owners need in 2026.
body_text: Your residents expect the internet to work the moment they walk through the door on move-in day. But choosing the right managed WiFi partner involves more than comparing bandwidth numbers on a proposal. The contract you sign today will shape your NOI, resident experience and operational headaches—or lack thereof—for the next five to 10 years. This guide walks you through the critical elements of managed WiFi contracts for multifamily properties: service level agreements, support models, ownership structures and the commercial terms that separate a genuine partnership from vendor lock-in. Elauwit Connection helps property owners navigate these decisions with honest technology advice tailored to current and future network needs. Whether you're evaluating your first managed WiFi deployment or renegotiating an existing agreement, the frameworks in this guide will help you ask the right questions and spot the terms that actually matter for your portfolio. Key Takeaways: How to Evaluate Managed WiFi Contracts in 2026 Service level agreements should include specific uptime guarantees with automatic credits—99.9% uptime is standard, with meaningful penalties for violations. Support quality matters more than support promises—evaluate response times, escalation paths, and whether you reach live humans or automated systems. Network ownership terms determine your flexibility at contract end—understand who owns the infrastructure and what happens during a provider transition. Elauwit Connection delivers 24/7 resident support with average answer times in less than 30 seconds, backed by public-company accountability. Contract length and exit provisions deserve as much scrutiny as pricing—negotiate buyout options and performance-based termination rights upfront. What Is a Managed WiFi Contract for Multifamily Properties? A managed WiFi contract is an agreement between a property owner and a connectivity provider covering the design, installation, operation and ongoing support of a property-wide wireless network. Unlike traditional bulk internet deals where you simply resell ISP service, managed WiFi contracts create an infrastructure partnership with defined responsibilities on both sides. The contract scope typically includes network design and engineering, hardware procurement and installation, 24/7 monitoring and maintenance, firmware updates and security patches, and direct resident support. Your provider handles the technical complexity while you focus on property operations. These agreements generally run five to 10 years. That timeline reflects the significant infrastructure investment involved—fiber backbone installation, access point deployment throughout units and amenity areas, and integration with property management systems. The length also means contract terms matter enormously. A bad deal locks you in, while a good one creates genuine value for years. Why Contract Terms Matter More Than Marketing Claims Every managed WiFi provider promises fast speeds, reliable service and responsive support. Those claims are table stakes. The difference between providers shows up in the contract details—the specific commitments, remedies and terms that determine what happens when things go wrong or your needs change. Marketing materials describe ideal scenarios. Contracts govern real-world accountability. When your network goes down during a lease-up weekend, the marketing brochure won't help. Your SLA terms will determine how quickly someone responds and what compensation you receive. Property owners who treat contracts as formalities end up with regret. Those who negotiate thoughtfully—with clear understanding of what they need and what the market offers—build connectivity infrastructure that genuinely supports NOI and resident satisfaction for years. How Should You Evaluate Service Level Agreements for Managed WiFi? Service level agreements define the provider's performance commitments in measurable terms. A strong SLA transforms vague promises into enforceable obligations. A weak one gives you nothing to hold onto when service falls short. Uptime Guarantees and What They Actually Mean The standard industry benchmark is 99.9% uptime, sometimes called "three nines." This sounds impressive until you calculate what it allows: roughly 8.7 hours of downtime per year. For a property with hundreds of residents working from home, streaming entertainment and relying on connected devices, 8.7 hours of outage is significant. When evaluating uptime guarantees, look beyond the percentage. Ask how uptime is measured—does the provider use their own monitoring tools or independent verification? What counts as an outage? Some contracts define downtime narrowly, excluding "scheduled maintenance" windows that could add hours of annual interruption. Also clarify what the guarantee applies to. Property-wide outages are one thing. But what about partial outages affecting specific buildings or floors? The best SLAs address both scenarios with specific commitments. Credit Structures That Create Real Accountability Uptime guarantees mean nothing without consequences for missing them. SLA credits are the mechanism that creates provider accountability. Review the credit structure carefully. Meaningful credits typically start at 10% of monthly service fees for each violation, escalating with repeated misses. Some providers cap total credits at one month's fees per year—which may be reasonable or may limit your recourse if service consistently underperforms. Automatic credits demonstrate provider confidence. If they require you to document outages, submit claims and wait for review, you'll rarely see compensation even when it's warranted. Automatic crediting based on their own monitoring data shows they stand behind their commitments. Speed Guarantees and Peak Performance Standards Advertised speeds create expectations. Contract guarantees determine whether those expectations are met. Push for specific minimum speed commitments—typically 80% of advertised bandwidth—measured at the unit level during peak usage hours. Peak hours matter because network performance degrades when everyone comes home from work, starts streaming and loads up their connected devices. A provider delivering 900 Mbps at 2 a.m. but 200 Mbps at 8 p.m. isn't meeting resident expectations, regardless of what the marketing says. Testing methodology should be defined in the contract. Independent speed tests from resident devices provide more meaningful data than measurements at the network switch. Specify how and when testing occurs, and what happens when results fall short. What Support Models Should You Require in a Managed WiFi Contract? Support quality separates tolerable connectivity from genuinely good resident experience. Your managed WiFi provider's support model determines whether network issues become property management headaches or get resolved before your leasing team ever hears about them. 24/7 Availability and What It Actually Means Every provider claims 24/7 support, but few deliver it equally. Ask specifically who answers calls at 2 a.m. on a Sunday—is it a trained technician or an answering service taking messages? What escalation authority do after-hours staff have? Response time commitments should be explicit in the contract. For critical issues affecting the entire property, four-hour response is a reasonable expectation. For individual unit problems, next-business-day may be acceptable depending on your resident population and expectations. Elauwit Connection maintains regional service hubs staffed with technicians who can respond quickly to portfolio properties. Real humans answer in less than 30 seconds on average—a concrete commitment that contrasts sharply with industry-standard call center experiences. Resident Support vs. Property Team Support Clarify who handles what. Does your provider support residents directly, or do connectivity complaints flow through your property management team? The answer affects your operational burden significantly. Direct resident support from your managed WiFi provider keeps internet complaints off your leasing team's plate. When residents can call a dedicated support line and reach someone who can actually help, your staff spends time on leasing and community management instead of troubleshooting router issues. The contract should specify support scope for both audiences. Property teams need different support than residents—faster response times, direct technical escalation paths and reporting on network-wide issues. Make sure both are addressed. Escalation Paths and Account Management When standard support channels fail, you need escalation options. The contract should define who owns your relationship and how to reach them when routine support isn't resolving an issue. Dedicated account managers make a meaningful difference, particularly for portfolio operators managing multiple properties. Having a named contact who understands your communities and can coordinate across locations eliminates the frustration of explaining your situation repeatedly to different support representatives. For critical situations—network-wide outages, security incidents or issues affecting lease-up timelines—executive escalation should be available. Some providers offer direct access to leadership for portfolio clients. Others route everything through standard support channels regardless of severity. How Do Ownership and Infrastructure Terms Affect Your Flexibility? Network ownership is one of the most consequential—and least discussed—elements of managed WiFi contracts. Who owns the infrastructure determines your options at contract end, your ability to switch providers and your control over the network serving your residents. Provider-Owned vs. Property-Owned Infrastructure In provider-owned models, the managed WiFi company owns all network equipment—fiber, switches, access points and in-unit hardware. You pay a monthly service fee that covers both connectivity and equipment. When the contract ends, they can remove their equipment, leaving you to start fresh with a new provider. Property-owned models give you the infrastructure. You may pay higher upfront costs for equipment, but you own assets that stay with the building regardless of which provider operates the network. This approach offers more flexibility but requires capital investment. Hybrid models exist as well. Some providers offer Network-as-a-Service options with zero upfront capital, while others support owner-funded builds. Elauwit Connection offers flexible ownership and financing options to match your capital plan—you choose the structure that fits your asset strategy. Transition Rights and Provider Changes Contracts end. Providers get acquired. Circumstances change. Your contract should address what happens when you need to transition to a new provider. Key questions: What is the process for terminating service? What notice is required? Does the provider assist with transition, or do they simply disconnect? For provider-owned infrastructure, can you purchase equipment at fair market value rather than starting from scratch? Exit provisions deserve as much attention as initial pricing. A contract with favorable monthly rates but punitive early termination fees and no transition assistance locks you in even when service falls short. Negotiate buyout options at specific intervals—years three and five are common checkpoints—with declining penalties over time. Infrastructure Documentation and Handoff Whether you own the network or not, you need documentation. As-built drawings, equipment inventories, configuration backups and maintenance records should be contractually required deliverables. This documentation protects you during provider transitions, supports your property team's understanding of the network and provides critical information for future upgrades or expansions. A provider unwilling to commit to thorough documentation raises questions about their long-term partnership orientation. What Commercial Terms Shape the True Cost of Managed WiFi? Per-unit pricing is the number everyone focuses on, but total cost depends on a range of commercial terms that may not appear prominently in the initial proposal. Understanding these terms helps you compare providers accurately and avoid unexpected expenses. Base Service Fees and What They Include Monthly per-unit fees typically range from $25 to $50 for managed WiFi service, depending on speed tiers, provider and portfolio size. But "per-unit fee" can mean different things across providers. Clarify what's included. Does the fee cover equipment, or is that separate? What about installation? Support? Premium SLA tiers? Some providers bundle everything into a single per-unit rate. Others price components separately, making apples-to-apples comparison difficult. Also confirm how fees are calculated. Do you pay for occupied units only, or all units? What about model units, vacant units or amenity spaces? These details affect your actual monthly expense. Installation and Infrastructure Costs Upfront installation costs vary dramatically based on building condition, existing wiring and scope of work. New construction deployments integrated during the build process differ significantly from retrofits requiring extensive cabling work in occupied communities. Get fixed-price quotes for installation rather than estimates. Unexpected costs during deployment create budget problems and strained relationships. Reputable providers conduct thorough site assessments before quoting and stand behind their numbers. Network assessment fees, permit costs and riser construction charges may appear as separate line items. For portfolio deals, these should typically be waived or heavily discounted. Push back on fees that feel like padding. Revenue Sharing and NOI Contribution Managed WiFi can contribute to NOI through revenue sharing arrangements, bulk billing models or amenity fee structures. The contract should clearly define the economic model. In revenue-sharing arrangements, you receive a portion of what residents pay for upgraded service tiers. The split varies—50/50 is common, though larger portfolios may negotiate more favorable terms. The contract should specify how revenue is calculated, when payments are made and what reporting you receive. Bulk billing models allow you to include internet in rent or charge it as a mandatory amenity fee. The spread between what you pay the provider and what you charge residents becomes direct NOI contribution. Elauwit Connection helps owners capture this value—properties typically see 200-300 basis points of NOI improvement from well-structured managed connectivity. Price Escalation and Long-Term Cost Predictability A five-year contract with 5% annual escalation costs 27% more in year five than year one. Understand how prices change over time and negotiate caps on increases. Annual escalation tied to CPI (Consumer Price Index) provides some predictability while acknowledging inflation. Fixed percentage caps—2-3% annually—give you more budget certainty. Some providers offer locked pricing for the full contract term in exchange for longer commitments. For portfolio acquisitions, negotiate price protection for properties you add during the contract term. Locking in current per-unit rates for future additions—typically with 12-24 month windows—protects you from price increases as your portfolio grows. How Do You Evaluate Provider Financial Stability and Track Record? Managed WiFi contracts create long-term dependencies. A provider that fails, gets acquired or changes strategic direction mid-contract creates significant problems for your properties and residents. Evaluating financial stability and track record helps you avoid these situations. Public Company vs. Private Provider Considerations Public companies offer transparency through required financial disclosures. You can review audited financials, understand debt levels and assess business trajectory before signing. This visibility provides comfort that your provider will still be operating five years from now. Elauwit Connection is the only publicly traded managed services provider dedicated exclusively to residential communities, trading on Nasdaq under ticker ELWT. This public-company accountability means audited financials, disclosed performance metrics and operational discipline that private companies may lack. Private providers can be excellent partners, but require more due diligence. Ask about recent funding rounds, investor backing and years in operation. Request references from customers with similar portfolio profiles and contract lengths. References and Portfolio Experience Ask for references specifically from operators managing portfolios similar to yours—comparable unit counts, property types and geographic markets. A provider excelling in student housing may struggle with luxury lease-ups. One dominating the Southeast may have limited capabilities in your markets. Reference calls should cover both good times and bad. How did the provider handle installation delays? Network outages? Difficult residents? Support escalations? The answers reveal more than any marketing pitch. With 38,000+ units under contract across 25 states and 20+ years exclusively in residential, Elauwit has developed deep fluency in how properties actually operate. That experience shows in deployment efficiency, support quality and understanding of what property teams need. Technology Roadmap and Future-Proofing Network technology evolves quickly. The WiFi 6 standard deployed today will be superseded by WiFi 7 and whatever comes next. Your provider's technology roadmap determines whether your network remains current or becomes obsolete mid-contract. Ask how the provider handles technology upgrades. Are access point replacements included in your service fees? What triggers an upgrade? How do they evaluate and deploy new standards? Providers investing in their own infrastructure—rather than simply reselling incumbent ISP services—typically deliver better upgrade paths. They control their technology stack and can deploy improvements without coordinating with third parties. What Questions Should You Ask During Managed WiFi Vendor Evaluation? The RFP process works best when you ask specific questions that reveal meaningful differences between providers. Generic questions get generic answers. Pointed questions surface the details that matter. Questions About Service Delivery Start with the basics of how they'll serve your properties: What is your deployment timeline from contract signature to resident activation? How do you handle existing ISP relationships and disconnect coordination? What bandwidth do you guarantee to each unit during peak hours, and how is that tested? Describe your network monitoring capabilities and how you proactively address issues before residents notice them. Questions About Support and Operations Dig into how support actually works: Who answers resident support calls at 10 p.m. on Saturday? What is your average response time for after-hours calls? How do you handle escalations when standard support isn't resolving an issue? What reporting do you provide on support volume, resolution times and network performance? Questions About Contract Terms Get specific about the commercial relationship: What are your standard contract length and early termination terms? How have you structured exit provisions for comparable portfolios? What happens to network infrastructure if we decide to change providers? How do you handle price increases during the contract term? Questions About Their Business Understand who you're partnering with: How is your company funded, and what's your financial trajectory? Who are your largest customers, and can you provide references? What percentage of your business is residential multifamily versus other segments? How has your technology platform evolved over the past three years? How Should You Structure the Contract Negotiation Process? Negotiating managed WiFi contracts requires preparation, leverage and patience. Providers expect negotiation—their initial proposals leave room for it. Rushing through this phase leaves value on the table. Building Leverage Through Competition Request proposals from at least three qualified providers. Even if you have a strong preference, competitive tension improves your outcome. Providers who know they're competing sharpen their pricing and terms. Share your evaluation criteria transparently. When providers understand what you prioritize—support quality over lowest price, for example—they can tailor proposals accordingly. This saves time and surfaces real differences. Prioritizing What Matters Most Not everything is equally negotiable. Providers have more flexibility on some terms than others. Identify your priorities and focus negotiating energy there. Per-unit pricing often has less room for movement than people expect—margins in managed WiFi aren't enormous. But installation costs, escalation caps, SLA credits and exit provisions often have significant flexibility. Trade-offs between categories can create wins for both parties. Getting Terms in Writing Verbal commitments made during sales conversations don't bind anyone. Every important term should appear in the contract itself—the main service agreement, SLA exhibit and any referenced schedules. Read the entire document, including standard terms and conditions. Providers sometimes bury unfavorable provisions in boilerplate language. Have legal counsel review the agreement before signing, particularly for larger portfolio deals. What Red Flags Should Disqualify a Managed WiFi Provider? Some warning signs should end your evaluation immediately. Recognizing red flags early saves time and prevents costly mistakes. Vague SLAs Without Specific Metrics If a provider can't define uptime guarantees, speed minimums and support response times in specific, measurable terms, their commitments mean nothing. Vagueness in the SLA predicts vagueness in actual service delivery. Resistance to Third-Party Testing Providers confident in their service quality welcome independent verification. Those who resist third-party speed testing or insist their own measurements are the only valid standard have something to hide. Exclusive Marketing Rights Contracts that require you to exclusively promote the provider's brand to residents, limit your communications or prevent you from discussing service issues with prospective providers create unhealthy relationships. Reasonable marketing cooperation is fine; restrictive exclusivity is not. Financial Instability or Acquisition Risk Providers with recent layoffs, executive departures or rumors of sale create contract continuity risk. While acquisition isn't always negative, entering a long-term agreement with a company likely to change ownership introduces uncertainty. Building a Connectivity Partnership That Supports Your Portfolio Managed WiFi contracts are infrastructure decisions that shape resident experience and property economics for years. Treating the contract as mere paperwork guarantees regret. Investing in thoughtful evaluation and negotiation creates genuine partnership. The providers who earn your business will demonstrate specific, enforceable commitments through their SLAs. They'll show support quality through references and concrete response time data. They'll offer ownership and transition terms that protect your flexibility. And they'll stand behind their proposals with the financial stability to be around for the contract's duration. Elauwit Connection approaches managed WiFi as a long-term infrastructure partnership, not a transactional service. With public-company accountability, 38,000+ units under contract across 25 states, and resident support that actually answers the phone, we've built a model that delivers for property owners and their residents. Contact us to discuss how managed WiFi can fit your portfolio's connectivity strategy. FAQs About How to Evaluate Managed WiFi Contracts in 2026 What uptime guarantee should I require in a managed WiFi SLA? The industry standard is 99.9% uptime, which allows approximately 8.7 hours of downtime annually. Make sure your contract includes automatic credits for violations—typically 10% of monthly fees per incident—rather than requiring you to document and claim credits manually. How do managed WiFi ownership models affect my property? Provider-owned infrastructure means lower upfront costs but less flexibility at contract end. Property-owned models require capital investment but give you assets that stay with the building. Elauwit Connection offers both approaches, letting you match the structure to your capital plan. What support response times should I expect from managed WiFi providers? For property-wide critical issues, four-hour response is reasonable. For individual unit problems, next-business-day may be acceptable. Elauwit delivers 24/7 support with real humans answering in less than 30 seconds on average—significantly faster than industry norms. How long do managed WiFi contracts typically last? Most contracts run five to 10 years, reflecting the infrastructure investment involved. Negotiate buyout options at years three and five with declining penalties. Performance-based termination rights give you exit options if the provider consistently misses SLA commitments. What should I look for in managed WiFi provider references? Ask for references from operators with similar portfolio profiles—comparable unit counts, property types and markets. Focus reference calls on how the provider handled problems: installation delays, outages and difficult support situations reveal more than success stories. How does managed WiFi contribute to property NOI? Managed WiFi contributes to NOI through the spread between provider costs and what you charge residents via rent inclusion or amenity fees. Elauwit Connection helps owners structure deals that deliver 200-300 basis points of NOI improvement through compelling property economics. What technology standards should I require in 2026? WiFi 6 is the current baseline, with WiFi 6E adding valuable spectrum for high-density environments. Your contract should address how technology upgrades are handled and funded. Providers investing in their own infrastructure typically offer better upgrade paths than those reselling incumbent ISP services.

title: LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox Review and Alternatives (2026)
summary: Is LegalZoom's virtual mailbox worth the money? We review how it works, what it costs, and whether it’s the right fit for your business.
body_text: What is LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox? The LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox is a business address service that lets users receive, view, and manage their mail online. It’s powered by Earth Class Mail, a company LegalZoom acquired to extend its business formation ecosystem beyond legal filings. The idea is simple: customers get a professional address where all mail is received, scanned, and uploaded to a digital dashboard. It’s positioned as a convenient add-on for new businesses that want to keep their legal, compliance, and correspondence tools under one roof. How does LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox work? LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox follows a straightforward process built around four steps: Choose your business address. You pick from more than 50 real street addresses across 44 states, including well-known business areas like Park Avenue in New York or Market Street in San Francisco. Mail is received securely. All business mail sent to your chosen address is handled by LegalZoom’s mail partners at processing facilities staffed by trained specialists. Your mail is digitized. Each piece is scanned and uploaded as a high-quality PDF to your online mailbox, with junk mail filtered out automatically. Access it all online. From there, you can read, forward, download, or request shredding directly from your dashboard. LegalZoom also offers check deposit and document sharing features. It’s a familiar setup that delivers convenience, but it lacks the depth and automation found in newer, software-native mailroom tools. Who is this virtual mailbox best for? LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox mainly appeals to small business owners and early-stage founders who already use LegalZoom for incorporation or registered agent services. It’s designed for those who value having everything from formation documents to compliance notices, and mail in one familiar dashboard. It’s less suited to teams that handle higher mail volumes or want collaborative tools for routing and managing correspondence. In those cases, dedicated virtual mailbox platforms built for automation and team workflows are a better fit. LegalZoom mail handling features LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox covers the basics of mail management, including scanning, digital access, and junk mail filtering. It’s functional but fairly traditional, relying on manual sorting and standard notifications to keep users informed. You can view documents from any device, share them with teammates, and even request check deposits, which works fine for small teams handling light correspondence. Where it starts to feel limited is in automation. There’s no intelligent routing or search functionality, meaning users still spend time manually deciding what’s important and who should handle it. By contrast, Postal’s AI mailroom service automates those steps entirely. The platform analyzes mail content, extracts deadlines, flags priorities, and forwards each item to the right teammate automatically. It’s a more modern approach designed for distributed teams that want their physical mail to function like email. That means organized, searchable, and instantly actionable. Security LegalZoom takes a conventional approach to mail security. The platform uses encryption, two-factor authentication, and secure facilities through its mail partners to protect incoming correspondence. For small businesses concerned mainly with privacy, for instance, keeping a home address off public records, it offers enough peace of mind to feel legitimate. Still, it’s not built for regulated industries or teams that manage sensitive information. There’s no published detail on compliance standards such as HIPAA or SOC 2, which limits its credibility for businesses handling client data, healthcare documents, or financial records. Postal’s HIPAA and SOC 2 compliant infrastructure sets a different bar. It identifies and redacts sensitive information like PHI and PII in real time, ensuring no confidential data is exposed during AI analysis. With dedicated compliance workflows and on-site secure scanning, Postal aligns mail handling with the same data protection standards most businesses already apply to their digital systems. User interface The LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox experience feels dated compared to modern business tools. Documents are accessible and navigation is straightforward, but it’s built on the same infrastructure as Earth Class Mail, which shows its age. Pages can load slowly, and the interface feels more transactional than intuitive. It’s clear the mailbox product was bolted onto LegalZoom’s broader system rather than designed as a cohesive software experience. The platform is “easy enough” to use, but occasionally clunky, especially when waiting for documents to appear or dealing with uploads that take longer than expected. It’s fine for occasional use, but teams that rely on daily mail management may find the interface too rigid for modern workflows. Postal, on the other hand, approaches this from a software-first perspective. Its interface is faster, cleaner, and designed for constant interaction. Think of it as treating mail like searchable, collaborative data rather than scanned PDFs. The difference in usability alone can make day-to-day operations far smoother, particularly for distributed teams managing mail at scale. LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox competitors and alternatives Weighing LegalZoom against dedicated providers? Here are the leading options at a glance. Provider Best for Key features Pricing Postal Modern businesses and remote teams. AI summaries and deadline alerts, natural-language search, PHI/PII recognition, and HIPAA & SOC 2 alignment. - Startup $49/month. - Scaleup $89/month - Enterprise (custom fee) - First 6 months free. Stable Startups that want a dependable address plus automations. Auto open/scan/ship, tags and assignments, search, Slack/Notion integrations, and API/webhooks. - Grow $49/month (annual). - Scale $83/month (annual). - Custom for enterprise. PostScan Mail Individuals and small teams on simple plans. U.S. street addresses, scan/forward/shred, and mobile apps. - Starter $10/month. - Standard $20/month. - Premium $30/month. iPostal1 Flexible location needs and low entry pricing. 3,500+ global addresses, mobile access, and optional phone/fax. - Mailing Address from $9.99/month. - Business $14.99/month. - Virtual Office $39.99/month. Anytime Mailbox Freelancers and businesses prioritizing location choice. 2,500+ locations, view/scan/forward, and mobile management. From $9.99/month (varies by location/tier). US Global Mail Expats, teams, and enterprises needing fast turnaround. Quick scans, unlimited exterior scans, check deposit, and 200+ integrations. - Essentials from $19.95/month. - Virtual Teams $45/month. Enterprise $85/month. Read our guide on the best virtual mailbox providers to explore how these services compare in greater depth. LegalZoom virtual mail pricing LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox is offered across three monthly plans. Each includes one business address, junk mail filtering, free shredding, and cloud storage, with differences based on mail volume and user access. Starter Mailbox – $29/month: For solo business owners and remote professionals. It includes 1 business address, 2 recipients, 5 mail items per month, free shredding, 30-day storage, and optional check deposits (additional fees apply). Essentials MailBox – $39/month: Designed for small teams managing moderate mail volumes. This tier includes 1 address, 5 recipients, 25 mail items per month, free shredding, 30-day storage, and access to virtual mail specialists. Premium Mailbox – $79/month: Aimed at businesses handling higher volumes. The highest-level plan comes complete with 1 address, 20 recipients, 50 mail items per month, free shredding, 30-day storage, and priority support. Extra fees apply for forwarding, check deposits, and storage beyond 30 days. While the plans are simple enough, they don’t offer the same long-term value as newer, software-driven alternatives. Postal, for example, charges a flat $49/month with the first six months completely free. It includes automation, AI features, and collaboration tools. Postal also provides free registered agent services in New York and California, where LegalZoom charges separately. Frequently asked questions about LegalZoom If you’re considering LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox, it’s worth clearing up some of the questions business owners ask most. Here’s a quick rundown of the most common ones and what to know before subscribing. Is LegalZoom virtual mailbox the same as Earth Class Mail? No, but they’re closely connected. LegalZoom acquired Earth Class Mail and now uses its infrastructure to power the LegalZoom Virtual Mailbox. The experience feels similar, though it’s integrated into LegalZoom’s wider business formation tools rather than functioning as a standalone platform. Is LegalZoom legit? Yes, LegalZoom is a legitimate and well-established company. It’s trusted for business formation and legal services, with secure processes and verified mail handling. That said, its virtual mailbox isn’t as advanced or automation-focused as modern, software-native alternatives. How much does LegalZoom cost? LegalZoom’s virtual mailbox starts at $29 per month for the Starter plan, $39 for Essentials, and $79 for Premium. Each tier adds more recipients and monthly mail items, but automation remains limited compared to platforms like Postal, which offers a flat $49/month plan with the first six months free.

title: The first idempotency key
summary: Discovering what we've all copied from Xerox.
body_text: Alexander Belanger Co-Founder Hatchet After reading Caity Weaver’s “ I Found It: The Best Free Restaurant Bread in America ”—a hero’s journey that starts with a rather simple question, posed at a local favorite restaurant, and ends with considerations of bread’s place in American culture—I realized two things. First, that I, too, greatly value a restaurant’s offering of free bread. Second, she and I share an interest in exploring seemingly trivial and impossible questions, such as is this the best free restaurant bread in America? As a software engineer, I often find myself wondering if the thing I’m looking at is the first instance of that thing. In other words, is this thing—usually a feature, product or platform— truly novel ? So as I was drafting up a post about our latest feature, idempotency keys , I set out to answer one such question: what was the first instance of an idempotency key? What’s an idempotency key? Idempotency keys are unique identifiers that allow API handlers or downstream consumers to de-duplicate messages that have been delivered more than once. If the handler has seen that string before, it’ll ignore the message. Consider my dog, Ringo (this is going somewhere, I promise). Ringo really likes his kibble (shoutout to Purina Pro Plan 30/20 Sport), so much so that exactly at 6pm, he’ll wake up from a coma-like slumber, grab his slow feeder bowl, and drop it at my feet. Ringo’s a sneaky bastard. He’ll get his dinner from me, and then amble into the adjacent room to beg his (non-biological) mother for more food. He knows that she doesn’t know he’s already been fed. On more than one occasion, he’s gotten double dinner. If my wife and I were a web server, we’d store an idempotency key to record the first instance of the meal. Instead we resort to yelling “I’M FEEDING RINGO” two times a day. Ringo with his pizza toy after being denied a second dinner. (For a deeper dive on how to implement a system like this on an actual web server, I’m a fan of this post .) Idempotency keys are a method of solving a fundamental problem in distributed systems, which is that exactly-once delivery is impossible, and we need some additional tooling to guarantee exactly-once processing . Ringo with his food bowl is an at-least-once delivery. My yelling guarantees exactly-once processing. With me so far? Stripe and AWS I live in Claude now, so naturally I asked it first: “When was the first instance of an idempotency key?” It responds: Around 2011, with Stripe’s Idempotency-Key header. I don’t know if this is accurate or not, but I like to test Claude. Sun Tzu puts it, “So in war, the way is to avoid what is strong, and strike at what is weak.” As in battle, so in Claude chat. My next move, a bluff: This is wrong. Both the date and the provider. And Claude says: Fair pushback—and I should own something here: my previous answer presented a confident single fact where none really exists. Searching now, I can’t find any authoritative record of a “first” idempotency key. Stripe popularized the name, but I was wrong to state it as the origin—and the “2011” date was my inference, not a documented fact. There it is, humankind’s small win for the day. Claude spews out some more random paragraphs and apologizes again. From what I can tell, Stripe’s Idempotency-Key header was published circa 2015 (though some blogs cite it without primary sources to be earlier). Stripe was indeed the first API I used which advertised this header. Good job Collisons. The Collison brothers, somewhere in between the younger one's birth and the invention of Stripe's Idempotency-Key header. Drunk with power, I bully Claude some more. It also cites Amazon EC2’s ClientToken behavior, which permitted clients to attach a unique string to mutating requests like RunInstances . If you use the same ClientToken with the same parameters, EC2 returns the original result; if you modify the parameters, you get an IdempotentParameterMismatch error. This behavior was recently codified in an IETF draft specification , which credits the idempotency patterns documented by Stripe, and also credits a 2005 Internet-Draft by Mark Nottingham called “POST Once Exactly.” I open my browser to read some old specs and forums, satisfied with my victory. POST Once Exactly POST Once Exactly, which you can find here , describes the motivating use-case for idempotency key behavior to be the following from the HTTP specification ( RFC 2616 ): Non-idempotent methods or sequences MUST NOT be automatically retried, although user agents MAY offer a human operator the choice of retrying the request(s). To solve this problem, in the POE specification, it’s proposed that a client issues a GET request first, which retrieves a POST URL. This POST URL must only accept a single successful POST. The “idempotency key” (note: this isn’t explicitly what it’s called in Nottingham’s implementation) is the unique part of the URL. POE wasn’t widely adopted, but it’s one of the first specifications I could find with some guidelines on how a RESTful API could easily implement idempotency-key behavior. Idempotency at the transport level Going back to ancient times of the early 2000s—a time of the spec wars between SOAP and REST—there were a number of abstruse specifications that aimed to implement exactly-once-processing with idempotency-key behavior. Two of these were the OASIS ebXML Message Service spec and the related WS-ReliableMessaging, co-published by Microsoft, IBM, BEA, and TIBCO. These are “transport-level” specifications, so if a service defines its contract as NoDuplicateDelivery , the transport implements message deduplication. Compare this with the RESTful way of doing things, where the application (or business layer) would send a custom header back to the client, and the business layer would decide how to handle this custom header in a future request. Whether exactly-once-processing should be handled at the transport layer is an interesting question; this article is a good read. Anyway, after spending an afternoon reading the OASIS ebXML spec and Microsoft’s WS-ReliableMessaging, I came to the realization that WS-ReliableMessaging was released for two reasons: (1) Microsoft was butthurt that it wasn’t in the conversation, and (2) they wanted to make reliable messaging more confusing. I Google pictures of sweaty Steve Ballmer to feel better. Steve Ballmer, likely punching his fist in victory after publishing WS-ReliableMessaging. Why am I writing this? The more I think about it, the more I realize humanity has invented and re-invented idempotency guarantees thousands of times throughout the years. The Incas, for example, used quipu —a sophisticated knot-tying system—to record important data like census counts, labor obligations, and inventories. In the mit’a labor obligation system, it was expected that able-bodied men would provide their labor to community projects on a rotational system. It would be recorded when a community received their labor obligation in the knot record; if they returned with another request, it would be denied. An Inca quipu Another example could be tally sticks, splitting a notched piece of wood down the middle between a creditor and a debtor, the number of notches representing the debt. In order to establish that the debt was repaid, the grain of both halves of the stick would be joined and need to match. (Granted, one could try to create a fake stick. Or you could lose your stick.) Admittedly I’ve lost the plot a bit. Do I really want my “final answer” to be an Incan quipu? Was the Incan empire perhaps the first example of a distributed system? A computer, even? No, I need something that rules out the incas, ledgers, a random thought about carrier pigeon networks, and my wife and I yelling at each other in our apartment. New rule: idempotency keys must touch electronic computers. I do some more research, which finally brings me to a fascinating and salient paper… Birrell and Nelson’s “Implementing RPCs” Well before the emergence of the internet and the world wide web, distributed systems research was built around the remote procedure call (RPC), which aimed to solve the problem of invoking a specific function (or procedure) on a different machine, usually within a trusted network. These RPC implementations were packages that were tightly coupled to a runtime or environment, like the Cedar programming environment at Xerox PARC —an experimental language and development environment that powered much of PARC’s systems research in the early 1980s. One of the papers emerging from this research was Birrell and Nelson’s “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls,” published in 1984, which builds upon Bruce Jay Nelson’s original PhD thesis —where he coined the term Remote Procedure Call—to document an implementation of an RPC package for use in distributed computation at Xerox PARC. This paper outlines the earliest example that I can find of an “idempotency key,” which is a call identifier for each RPC. Here it is, my actual answer. I’ll let Birrell and Nelson tell it: The call identifier serves two purposes. It allows the caller to determine that the result packet is truly the result of his current call (not, for example, a much delayed result of some previous call), and it allows the callee to eliminate duplicate call packets (caused by retransmissions, for example)… The RPCRuntime on a callee machine maintains a table giving the sequence number of the last call invoked by each calling activity. When a call packet is received, its call identifier is looked up in this table. The call packet can be discarded as a duplicate (possibly after acknowledgment) unless its sequence number is greater than that given in this table. After all this “research,” I’m still not sure if this is the oldest example of idempotency keys that meets my criteria. But I do know that ours is the newest. Go check it out !

title: Vertiv Announces New, Smaller Models of High Power Density UPS Family
summary: Vertiv, formerly Emerson Network Power, today announced an extension of its Liebert® EXL S1 line of uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, adding 625, 750 and 800 kVA ratings designed for data centers and colocation facilities seeking to scale in smaller modules. The new systems are available now in North America, complementing the 1000, 1100 and 1200 kVA ratings. body_text: Columbus, Ohio [Dec. 12, 2017] – Vertiv, formerly Emerson Network Power, today announced an extension of its Vertiv™ Liebert® EXL S1 line of uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems, adding 625, 750 and 800 kVA ratings designed for data centers and colocation facilities seeking to scale in smaller modules. The new systems are available now in North America, complementing the 1000, 1100 and 1200 kVA ratings. In Europe, Middle East and Africa, the Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 is offered in 11 ratings, ranging from 100 to 1200 kVA. With a compact footprint up to 54 percent smaller than competitive models, and industry-leading power per square foot, the transformer-free Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 now supports a wider range of capacities and data center requirements with a reliable, flexible and efficient power system. “In today’s evolving IT environments, where every square foot is a potential source of revenue, optimization is as important as availability,” said Franco Costa, vice president and general manager, power, for Vertiv. “With this extension of our Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 UPS line, we are able to deliver a wider range of reliable, efficient solutions to customers who strive to optimize their infrastructure and operations.” The Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 also delivers the high efficiency – up to 99 percent – expected of a transformer-free UPS system. Various input/output options add flexibility and reduce capital and installation costs. As with previous models, customers can parallel up to eight separate units intelligently, optimizing performance by sharing loads across the system. The system’s touchscreen interface offers status at a glance, customizable views and multiple security options, and intelligent controls ensure seamless integration with multiple Vertiv and third-party building management and data center infrastructure management systems. All sizes of the Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 UPS are available with lithium ion battery options, Alber® battery monitoring and LIFE™ Services. For more information on the Vertiv Liebert EXL S1 and other UPS solutions from Vertiv, visit www.Vertiv.com . About Vertiv Vertiv designs, builds and services critical infrastructure that enables vital applications for data centers, communication networks and commercial and industrial facilities. Formerly Emerson Network Power, Vertiv supports today’s growing mobile and cloud computing markets with a portfolio of power, thermal and infrastructure management solutions including the Chloride®, Liebert®, NetSure™ and Trellis ™ brands. Sales in fiscal 2016 were $4.4 billion. For more information, visit Vertiv.com . CONTACT: Vince McMorrow T +614 383 1622 E Vince.McMorrow@Fahlgren.com

title: 7 Best Business Gas Only Credit Cards
summary: We rank 7 gas only business cards by controls, savings, and acceptance. AtoB locks cards to fuel-only with mobile auth and 42¢/gal savings. Compare today.
body_text: A gas only business credit card restricts employee purchases to fuel and approved vehicle expenses at the transaction level. Unlike standard business payment cards that only list the fueling merchant on a statement, these specialized fleet cards capture detailed information, including gallons purchased, fuel type, driver ID, and vehicle assignment. This guide compares the best fuel-only card options for businesses, explains what to evaluate before selecting a provider, and outlines how modern fleet fuel cards combine controls, reporting, and fuel rewards into one system. Why Gas Only Cards Are Important for Businesses A fuel-only business credit card gives fleet operators more visibility and control over driver spending than a traditional business credit card or consumer gas card. Instead of reviewing transactions after they occur, businesses can manage purchases proactively through restrictions and reporting tools. This is especially important for businesses with growing fuel expenses or multiple drivers using company vehicles. For many operations, a dedicated fleet fuel card program provides stronger controls and reporting than standard payment cards. Understanding how fuel cards save you money reveals that the benefits for fleet operations extend beyond simple restrictions: Spend control - Set limits on purchases to fuel and approved vehicle categories, helping fleets reduce unauthorized fuel purchases and driver misuse Transaction visibility - Capture detailed data, including driver name, vehicle ID, gallons purchased, fuel type, and location for every fill-up Per-gallon savings - Access discount networks that reduce fuel costs at thousands of truck stops nationwide Streamlined accounting - Eliminate paper receipt chasing with digital records, automated IFTA fuel tax reporting , and direct accounting integrations Failing to prevent fuel card fraud and unauthorized purchases drains fleet profits every year. Gas only cards address that problem directly by enforcing purchase rules at the point of sale, helping fleets identify suspicious activity before it affects broader fleet expense management and operational efficiency. What to Look for in a Gas Only Business Card Before selecting a card, fleet operators should evaluate several operational and financial factors. Acceptance and Discounts Open-loop cards backed by Mastercard or Visa provide broader acceptance at truck stops and retail fuel locations nationwide. Closed-loop cards may offer deeper discounts, but they limit where drivers can fuel. Some providers focus on branded fuel networks, while others prioritize independent truck stop partnerships and broader fuel acceptance. Different providers structure savings differently by offering any of the following: Flat per-gallon savings - Fixed discount amount on every gallon purchased Cash back percentages - Percentage-based rebates on total fuel spending Rebate programs - Delayed savings credited back to your account The size of the discount network matters because savings only help when drivers can access it along their actual routes. The right program depends on where your drivers fuel and how frequently they purchase diesel or gasoline. Controls, Fees, and Approval Strong spend controls let managers restrict purchases by type of fuel, set daily or weekly limits, enforce time-of-day rules, and whitelist specific merchants for each driver or vehicle. Review the complete fee schedule first before applying, including: Monthly account fees Per-card charges Transaction fees Setup costs Out-of-network penalties These charges can quickly erode any per-gallon savings, so look for a card company offering transparent pricing. Approval structures and underwriting requirements vary by provider, particularly for newer businesses or fleets with limited operating history. Meanwhile, prepaid or prefunded options like a fuel prepaid card may offer more flexible approval structures for newer businesses. Understanding the differences between secured and prepaid fuel cards and understanding how prepaid gas cards work can help businesses choose the right balance of flexibility, control, and approval requirements. 7 Best Options for Business Fuel Cards Each card below was evaluated on acceptance, discount depth, fee structure, controls, fraud protection, and credit reporting capabilities. ‍ Card Primary Focus Acceptance Key Feature AtoB Fuel Card Overall fleet needs Mastercard network Telematics fraud prevention Voyager Low fees Major truck stops No monthly fee WEX Fleet Card Broad coverage Wide network Tiered discounts Shell Fleet Card Shell locations Shell and broader network Intro discount period Coast Fuel Card App-based control Visa network Purchase authorization Fuelman Mastercard Comprehensive controls Mastercard network Detailed restrictions RoadFlex Customizable limits Visa network Per-vehicle controls ‍ AtoB Fuel Card: Best Overall for Fleets AtoB offers both credit and prefunded options designed for transportation businesses: AtoB Flex provides credit functionality with Experian reporting, while AtoB Unlimited supports prepaid fleet spending for businesses seeking additional payment flexibility. Both business gas cards allow fleets to make vehicle-related purchases anywhere Mastercard is accepted and provide access to discount networks with average savings of 42¢ per gallon* on truck diesel at participating truck stops. Advanced controls include: Fuel-only restrictions — Block all non-fuel purchases at the transaction level Telematics-based location validation — Verify vehicle proximity to fueling location Secure Card Unlock — Requires mobile app authorization before each transaction AtoB helps fleets manage spending and reduce operational friction through one centralized platform. Voyager (via P-Fleet) Voyager provides fuel management tools, spending controls, and reporting capabilities for fleets operating across participating truck stop and fuel networks. Savings structures vary by location and network participation, with additional controls available for fleet managers overseeing driver purchases and vehicle activity. WEX Fleet Card WEX offers fuel management tools, transaction reporting, and fuel discount programs through participating fueling networks. Savings may vary based on fuel volume, network participation, and fueling locations, while branded card options are available for fleets operating within preferred truck stop networks. Shell Fleet Card (Business Flex) Shell offers introductory fuel discounts during the early billing cycles, with ongoing savings subject to program terms and monthly fuel volume. Drivers can access both Shell locations and a broader participating fuel network, making the card a potential option for fleets operating across regional routes. Coast Fuel Card Coast operates on the Visa network and supports app-based purchase authorization for driver transactions. The platform includes fuel savings at participating locations along with additional expense management tools for vehicle-related purchases beyond fuel. Fuelman Mastercard Fuelman provides fuel management tools, spending controls, and broad acceptance through the Mastercard network. Businesses evaluating the platform should compare fee structures, reporting capabilities, and network participation requirements when assessing long-term operating costs. RoadFlex Fuelman provides fuel management tools, spending controls, and broad acceptance through the Mastercard network. Businesses evaluating the platform should compare fee structures, reporting capabilities, and network participation requirements when assessing long-term operating costs. How AtoB Prevents Fuel Card Misuse Most fuel cards rely on basic PIN protection that drivers can share or bypass, leaving fleets vulnerable to unauthorized purchases and making it harder to prevent fuel theft . Telematics and Transaction Controls Through telematics integrations, AtoB validates vehicle location tracking to verify that the authorized vehicle is within range of the truck stop for each transaction. The system also monitors fuel levels in real-time, automatically blocking pump transactions that exceed a vehicle's tank capacity. These controls work for both traditional diesel purchases and electric vehicle charging payments. Card Lock, Spend Rules, and Fraud Guarantee Secure Card Unlock keeps cards locked until the authorized driver unlocks them through the mobile app, helping fleets reduce unauthorized card usage. Fleet managers can set granular restrictions, including: Time-of-day windows - Limit transactions to specific hours Merchant category limits - Restrict which types of businesses can process charges Per-transaction caps - Set maximum dollar amounts for individual purchases Which Business Gas Card Is Right for You? Matching the right card to your operation, such as finding the best gas card for small business needs, mainly depends on fleet size, routes, and financial goals. For smaller operations prioritizing rewards over fleet controls, comparing options for the best business credit card for gas cash back can also help narrow the field. ‍ Fleet Type Priority Features Owner-operators and small fleets Broad acceptance, low operating costs, and flexible payment options Mid-size fleets Discount depth, telematics integration, and centralized reporting across all vehicles Businesses building credit Cards that report payment history to business credit bureaus like Experian ‍ The best prepaid fleet fuel cards work well for businesses seeking tighter spending controls and simplified budgeting. Credit-based cards, on the other hand, can improve cash flow through net payment terms while helping businesses build credit over time. The best business gas credit cards are the ones that align with your actual routes, fuel volume, and operational needs. Rather than focusing only on headline discounts, evaluate where your drivers fuel most often and whether the card’s savings, controls, and reporting features support your day-to-day operations. Frequently Asked Questions What is a gas only credit card for businesses? A gas only credit card for businesses restricts employee purchases to fuel while capturing detailed transaction data, including gallons, fuel type, price per gallon, driver ID, and vehicle assignment. These cards are available in both credit-based and prepaid formats. Can I get a business fuel card that works only at truck stops? Yes, closed-network fleet cards exist for truck stop-only use and often provide deeper diesel discounts. Universal cards like AtoB combine truck stop discounts with the flexibility to fuel at any location that accepts Mastercard. Is a prepaid fuel card better than a credit-based fleet card? Prepaid fuel cards require no credit check and provide exact budget control. Credit-based cards offer net payment terms, higher spending limits, and help build business credit through bureau reporting. Do gas only business credit cards offer rewards or discounts? Most business fuel cards let you earn per-gallon discounts or rebates rather than traditional rewards points. Compare discount depth, network size, and whether savings are capped per billing cycle. Apply for fuel cards now to start saving on every gallon. ‍ * Average discount of 42¢ refers to realized average savings per gallon of truck diesel across AtoB customer transactions at merchant partner truck stops during H2 2025. The up to discount of $2.00 refers to max realized savings per gallon of truck diesel across AtoB customer transactions at merchant partner truck stops during H2 2025. Average discount of 5¢ off per gallon of unleaded is an average across AtoB customer transactions at merchant partner gas stations during H2 2025. ‍

body_text: Press Releases Pega Drives Cash Flow and Releases AI Innovation in Q2 2026 Pega Cloud Annual Contract Value (ACV) increases 22% year over year ACV grows 7% year over year (8% in constant currency) Cash flow from operations and free cash flow both exceed $285M in first half of 2026 Clients react with enthusiasm to Pega’s ‘no per-token cost’ WALTHAM, Mass. — July 21, 2026 — Pegasystems Inc. (NASDAQ: PEGA), the Enterprise Transformation Company™, released its financial results for the second quarter of 2026. "Pega Infinity™ 26 uniquely deploys the power of AI with predictable outcomes and predicable costs by applying agents at design time to optimize run-time token use,” said Alan Trefler, founder and CEO, Pega. "Letting language models do everything is risky and expensive, and using AI to write mountains of code creates significant barriers to the ongoing change that enterprise clients require. Pega structures business applications in a way that makes sense to business and IT to Build for Change®.” "Pega generated record first-half cash flow and returned substantial capital to shareholders,” said Ken Stillwell, COO and CFO, Pega. “As the market shifts from AI experimentation to tokenomics and reliable business outcomes, that evolution plays directly to Pega’s strengths, and we remain confident in our strategy to capitalize on the opportunity ahead.” Financial and performance metrics (1) (1) Refer to the schedules at the end of this release for additional information, including a reconciliation of GAAP and non-GAAP measures.
